title: City of Monterey v. Del Monte Dunes at Monterey, Ltd.
lead: Repeated revisions failed to secure development approval, and the resulting takings damages suit raised whether a jury could decide the particular application’s contested facts.

actors.name: Del Monte Dunes and its predecessor
actors.role: Owners seeking development of an oceanfront parcel

actors.name: City of Monterey
actors.role: Land-use authority defending denial of the final plan

proceedings: District court initially dismissed as unripe; Ninth Circuit reversed.
On remand jury awarded $1.45 million on takings and equal protection; judge rejected substantive due process.
Ninth Circuit affirmed on takings; Supreme Court affirmed 5–4.
limits: The Court accepted the case’s ripeness posture and largely unchallenged substantive instructions rather than updating takings law. Part IV-A-2 had only four votes. Ordinary inverse condemnation and broader zoning jury allocations were reserved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The owners reduce their project repeatedly
sections.cue: The site combines development potential and habitat concerns
paragraphs: Del Monte Dunes and its predecessor sought housing on a 37.6-acre Monterey oceanfront parcel zoned for multifamily use and largely surrounded by developed and transportation uses. A former oil facility left debris and contaminated sand. Introduced ice plant threatened remaining vegetation, including buckwheat habitat for the endangered Smith’s Blue Butterfly. Surveys located only one larva, but habitat remained a regulatory concern.

The owners proposed 344 units in 1981, below potential zoning density. The planning commission rejected that plan and suggested 264, then rejected the revision and suggested 224. After another rejection, the council directed consideration of 190 units. Four plans followed. The commission rejected them, but the council conditionally approved one with an eighteen-month use permit.

Revisions supplied public open space, beach access, landscaping, view corridors, and habitat restoration, leaving only 5.1 acres for buildings and patios. Architectural review approved and planning staff recommended approval as substantially satisfying the conditions. Nonetheless the commission rejected it in January 1986, followed by the council, which refused further curative directions or a permit extension. It cited access, environmental layout, and habitat concerns the owners said earlier changes addressed. A sewer moratorium impeded restarting. After five years, five formal decisions, and nineteen plans, the owners concluded no development would be allowed.

sections.title: The damages action survives a ripeness dismissal
sections.cue: Accepted instructions frame the jury’s work
paragraphs: The owners sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for an uncompensated taking, equal protection, and substantive due process. The district court dismissed as unripe, but the Ninth Circuit found finality and no adequate California compensation remedy for temporary regulatory takings at the relevant time. The Supreme Court later accepted that established posture.

On remand, takings and equal protection went to a jury while the judge retained substantive due process. The jury could find a taking from loss of all economically viable use or failure of the final 190-unit denial substantially to advance a legitimate public purpose. Instructions accepted the legitimacy of environmental, open-space, safety, and community-quality goals and disputed only the connection of this denial to those goals. The City had proposed the essential instruction.

The jury found for the owners on both claims and awarded $1.45 million. The judge found for the City on due process and denied posttrial motions. The Ninth Circuit affirmed on takings without reaching equal protection. The City sought review of jury allocation, improper policy reconsideration, and the appellate reference to Dolan’s rough proportionality.

sections.title: The Court narrows the questions actually presented
sections.cue: The jury right comes from the Seventh Amendment
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy’s unanimous Part II rejected extending Dolan beyond development exactions to an outright denial. But the instructions did not use rough proportionality and the appellate discussion was unnecessary, so that error required no reversal. The Court also declined amici’s invitation to revise substantive takings precedents underlying the accepted instructions.

The jury was not assigned general zoning policy. The owners conceded legitimate regulatory purposes and challenged this particular final denial against the City’s own changing requirements. Neither general ordinance invalidity nor every imposed condition was at issue.

Section 1983’s reference to an action at law did not itself create a statutory jury guarantee. Five Justices instead treated a § 1983 claim for legal relief as tort-like under the Seventh Amendment. The owners sought compensation for denial of just compensation in the established absence of an adequate state remedy, not an ordinary government-initiated proceeding conceding liability and fixing price.

sections.title: Historical analogies divide the majority coalition
sections.cue: The specific liability issues remain appropriately factual
paragraphs: Only four Justices joined Kennedy’s Part IV-A-2 comparing historical tort and quasi-contract remedies for uncompensated property interference with an ordinary condemnation. The plurality saw a disputed denial of compensation and a forum, rather than government acknowledgment of a payment obligation. Public-use authority did not make nonpayment categorically lawful because compensation was an essential condition.

Justice Scalia preferred the general § 1983 tort-like cause of action over a new historical analogue for each constitutional right. Damages through that vehicle implicated the Seventh Amendment, though a purely equitable request did not acquire a jury simply from the tort analogy. He agreed the legitimacy of public purposes was legal and properly removed from the jury, while their relation to this specific refusal was sufficiently factual. He expressly withheld judgment on the forfeited substantive standard.

The controlling analysis found no exact historical counterpart but considered precedent and institutional process. Loss of all economically viable use was predominantly factual. The purpose-connection issue, though mixed, was tightly tied to this record. The Court reserved ordinary inverse-condemnation jury rights and precise allocation across broader zoning or regulatory challenges.

sections.title: Souter favors the condemnation analogy
sections.cue: The existing judgment is affirmed without another trial
paragraphs: Justice Souter, joined by O’Connor, Ginsburg, and Breyer, agreed with Parts I and II and the absence of a statutory jury right. He considered direct condemnation the closest analogue because both proceedings enforced compensation, and direct condemnation historically lacked a constitutional jury entitlement. Changing the initiator or distinguishing liability from damages did not persuade him. He rejected the broader § 1983 analogy and emphasized judicial competence in deferential government review.
His proposed remand need not retry facts: the district judge could treat the verdict as advisory and make independent findings. That was the dissent’s proposal, not the result.

On May 24, 1999, the Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit five to four, sustaining submission of this particular § 1983 damages claim to the jury. The $1.45 million judgment stood without a majority-ordered retrial or remand.
